RANK 8 (more) — Night Pla ([Sharing of Pain] — an active with a self-explanatory but undetailed effect). Ironhill Chaser (a penetration-on-surprise-attack passive, plus a three-color arrow kit — red penetrating, blue terrain-eruption, yellow weak-point).

RANK 7 (more) — Corpse Golem itself as an essence (distinct from its combat tactics already noted) carries no described skill beyond what's already covered under its bestiary entry. Ironro ([Counterweight] — total knockback immunity plus shock absorption while grounded, the actual named source of the "Ironrock Guardian" entry already listed). Hobgoblin (adds poison to the wearer's weapon). Orc High Shaman ([Imprint of Regeneration] — a strong single-target regeneration buff). Plminas ([Thunderthorn] — a lightning-charged thrown projectile). An unsourced Rank 7 essence, ["Overload"] (raises ranged damage at the cost of temporary weight gain and slowed movement — warriors specifically avoid it).

RANK 6 (more) — an unsourced ["Tail Flame"], effect undescribed beyond the name.

RANK 4 (more) — an unsourced ["Dark Veil"] (a translucent black barrier that blocks damage outright). An unsourced ["Bone Armor"] (grows heavy bone plating over the skin). An unsourced ["Blood System Entry"] (turns the wearer into a fast-moving blood mist immune to physical damage while active, at reduced strength). An unsourced ["Sublime Idol"] (a totem that converts a single buff or curse into a wide-area aura version of itself). An unsourced ["Residual Heat"] (bonus damage scaling with damage already dealt; against multiple fire-damaged targets, a partial-refund effect triggers). Three further unsourced Rank 4 essences: ["Weapons of War"] (temporary damage reduction after repeated attack-skill use), ["Indomitable Soul"] (a strong physical buff plus 80% resistance to behavior-restricting status effects), ["Endurance"] (resistances rise slightly whenever a defense attempt fails outright).

RANK 3 (more) — an unsourced ["Kinship"], effect undescribed. An unsourced ["Gate of Light"] — genuinely top-tier movement: wraps the body in light and moves it to any chosen point, not just a random short hop; capped uses per encounter with a cooldown after the third. Elder Lich ([Soul Extraction] — a single-target faint effect, counterable through mental resistance or magic resistance). Bandemon ([Grief Strike], undetailed beyond the name). Hellsmith ([Tapping] — a sustained fire-empowerment buff that keeps burning the surroundings; [Soldering] — a slower, silver-film wound seal).

RANK 2 (more) — four unsourced Rank 2 essences, all genuinely strong: ["Vampire Post"] (a low-cost, high-damage physical ranged strike with life-steal). ["Land End Thorns"] (a piercing black thorn attack, rated top-tier for this rank). ["Brain Step"] (a three-second blink followed by area paralysis on arrival, plus a movement and damage-immunity buff — release requires either landing the first hit or waiting out a duration). ["Conductor"]/["Thunder Cloud"] paired passive-active (stacks on lightning-skill use, feeds a wide lightning burst whose cooldown shrinks with stacks spent). ["Polar Charge"] (converts a lightning-linked self-damage effect into physical damage instead — a weapon-enchantment-type conversion skill). Balantis carries one further undetailed active, ["Future Confirmation"], beyond what's already listed. A final unsourced Rank 2, ["Lantern of Evil"] (swaps whatever field effect is active for a different one of the same severity).

RANK 1 (more) — a Rank 1 essence granting ["Clock Hand of Regret"] (when a soul-bonded companion dies, restart from an earlier fork in the fight — never triggers on the wearer's own death, months-long cooldown, three uses maximum lifetime). A second unsourced Rank 1 essence granting ["In the Airship"] (conjures a functional airship on demand — real, dramatic travel-time compression even without a sea route). Taurbrood/Taurburd's full kit is worth stating precisely: no passive at all, but seven named actives covering defense (a barrier), offense (a beam), mobility (a short blink with real drawbacks under restraint), and battlefield control (a stop-time effect against everyone but the caster and one target) — genuinely a complete build from a single essence, which is exactly why it's rated deceptively strong for its lack of a passive.

CONFIRMED REAL, NO DESCRIBED ABILITY. These names are genuine entries in the essence registry — not invented — but the source gives nothing beyond the name and, usually, the source monster's rank. Treat exactly like the undocumented monster names already noted: build fresh from rank alone if one ever matters in play, and hold it fixed once built. Rank 7: Bitol, Yeti, imp, sea worm. Rank 6: Cheongbaekgung Judge, gacha book. Rank 4: rich, night mare, Semura, medusa, Ritt Cannon, Gravanich, macrow. Rank 3: Bol-herchan, Celestial Judge, speardipper, Arbet (though its stats alone are confirmed to rival Rank 2), lamansis (confirmed exclusive-affinity-gated), Dreamer Mortis's core mechanic is already covered elsewhere.

entries.name: Noark — City & War History
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_STATE]
ORIGIN. An underground shelter, thousands of years old — predates Rafdonia and once functioned as the actual royal seat, before the surface city was built and the population moved up. Opening the portal that connects Noark to the Labyrinth requires the bloodline of Noark's own castle-lord specifically; it isn't a Rafdonia-style Dimensional Square anyone can walk through.

DAILY LIFE ("Noir" to its own residents). Genuinely more tolerant of Evil Spirits than Rafdonia — plenty of people here don't reject one on sight, or even hide what they are, and the general assumption that an open Evil Spirit must be a criminal doesn't really hold up against how ordinary the streets look: clean, calm, not visibly darker than anywhere else. Golem "patrol" units, all consecrated to the Holy Spirit, do the policing. Only one working alchemist exists, so the market is real but small, prices run high, and food mostly comes portioned rather than fresh — order ahead at the alchemy workshop, wait about two days, pay considerably more than the Rafdonia equivalent. It's taboo to lay a hand on a Noark-born "ordinary person" (non-explorer); the castle-lord punishes it, somehow, every time. Most jobs that aren't exploring are inside the castle itself. There's no Explorers' Guild here — a "labyrinth management" office does the same job, slower: new registration is separate, and the entry fee has to be paid fresh every single time you go down, unlike Rafdonia's one-time registration. The whole system is underfunded and understaffed enough that even basic requests (a party-solidarity spell, for one on-record case) can mean waiting an hour for a tired staff wizard to get back from a break. Crime is common enough that explorer brawls in the street aren't unusual.

THE WAR — deep spoiler-tier plot history. Never ambient knowledge for a fresh character; this is what a GM draws on if the topic gets investigated seriously in play, not something anyone just happens to know.
An Orcules team tracking Karui's priests broke through a sealed magical door underground and stumbled into Noark territory for the first time in generations. The immediate skirmish escalated into a full confrontation; a Ludwig of the Leautlas order sacrificed himself deep inside the Labyrinth of Larcaz to drag a threat back down with him, and his final letter — carried out by his own team — set off the actual war between the crown and Noark.
Noark answered with a coordinated strike during a monthly Labyrinth opening: infiltrators used the semi-independent, boundary-loose nature of Floor 4's Tower in the Sky to smuggle an assassin into a descending party. The resulting incident killed 471 explorers on Floor 4 alone — rated one of the worst single losses in Rafdonia's history.
A full Rafdonian expeditionary corps then descended into Noark itself. Both sides took catastrophic losses. Rafdonia: only about a third of the corps came back; three of the era's major clans were effectively wiped out (under 10% survival); most mid-sized Floor 5-6 clans took heavy losses too; public trust in the crown cracked hard. Noark: sealed itself off just short of total defeat, its remaining people given final orders before the gates shut.
Afterward, the crown throttled Noark's resource access and stationed a royal division to police Noark-born explorers still working the Labyrinth. Roughly six months later, coordinated with major clans boycotting the Labyrinth in protest, Noark forged fake identification and struck the surface directly: infiltrators fogged the first floor with a toxin-laced mist, picked off explorers in the nominal safe zones, and cut off the routes to Floor 2. The real objective was never the visible fighting — it was baiting enough of a crowd together to summon an extremely dangerous hidden-tier threat, while a separate team quietly destroyed the Floor 2 portal monument to trap everyone caught in the opening stages. Facing an unwinnable trade of casualties against sealing the immediate threat, Rafdonia's senior leadership made the call to abandon tens of thousands of ordinary explorers still trapped below in order to save the concentrated high-value clan and knight forces, and pulled the survivors out through a different route. What followed is remembered as the single worst night in Rafdonia's history — seven pillars of fire over the seven Dimensional Squares, roughly five thousand people lost in an instant, only about a hundred survivors at the very edge of the blast radius. Bjorn Yandel's own rise to prominence traces directly to being one of the very few explorers who chose to stay and fight rather than retreat with the abandoning forces.
The two sides fought to a standstill shortly after, until an unidentified figure intervened and stopped the battle outright, opening a path that ended the siege era entirely and let Noark step out from behind its walls for the first time in generations.

AFTERMATH. Even Noark-born residents can turn out to be Evil Spirits — nothing about growing up there makes it less possible.

USE IN PLAY. As ambient, safe-to-know background: Noark exists, is an underground city with its own history and its own relationship to the Labyrinth, was at open war with Rafdonia within living memory, and the war left both sides scarred. The specific chain of events above — the priests, Ludwig, the Floor 4 assassination, the abandonment, the seven pillars of fire — surfaces only through real in-fiction investigation, old survivors talking, restricted records, or similar earned discovery.

entries.name: Hierarchical Lords — Floor Bosses
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_STATE]
One per floor, roughly, plus one in the Basement. Not ordinary Rift Guardians — these are catastrophic, world-tier threats that roam a floor once summoned, closing portals and killing indiscriminately until put down. Genuinely reachable only by huge, well-organized raids; for anyone else, the correct move on hearing one is loose is to leave the floor. Treat all of this as background knowledge of what's actually out there, not a fight the player is expected to pick.

DREADFEAR — Floor 1, Lord of Fear. A twisted, corrupted pilgrim wearing a dead rival's name and face. Recalled repeatedly rather than permanently slain (roughly a 6-hour respawn once summoned); an ordinary kill yields almost nothing — no loot, no Numbered Items, only the achievement and a shot at clan advancement. Summonable only once five or more explorers linger in its territory past the third day. A five-person clear is a real historical benchmark — only a handful of raids have ever managed it, against the more usual thirty-plus needed. A specific hidden branch of this fight — reached only under a narrow, undocumented trigger condition — leads into the Pilgrim's Cave, a separate hidden field. Completing THAT path, not the ordinary kill, is what actually yields Numbered Item No. 12 (Trust) and opens access to Basement Floor 1.

BERZAC — Floor 1, Lord of the Abyss. Summoned only after Dreadfear has been killed nine times. Its true danger isn't raw power — eye contact stacks a fear debuff, and nine stacks means permanent, irreversible monsterization: the character simply becomes a hostile monster from then on. Its signature field effect nulls most active-skill usage and cuts magic efficiency to a quarter, which is why raids against it lean almost entirely on tanks, Aurors, and priests rather than casters.

REGRET — Floor 2, one Lord per each of the four regions.

LIAKIS (also spelled Riakis) — Floor 3, Lord of Chaos. Summoned by offering seven sacrifices at the Witch's Hut; once loose, it roams the whole floor, the Witch's Forest's own field effect cancels out, and portals between floors briefly stop working. A body roughly 30m across, multi-phase, escalating. The Numbered Item Torches of Purification (No. 8645) lets a raid skip the worst of one especially punishing phase-two trap without waiting out its full two-day duration. A clean kill permanently ends the threat and grants a large, flat achievement bonus — not a Numbered Item; that reward belongs to Dreadfear's separate Pilgrim's Cave path, not to this fight.

LORD OF THE SKY — Floor 4, guards the Tower in the Sky. Killing it lets the raid choose one permanent active effect as a reward.

CILIOT — Floor 5, Lord of Silence. Nulls all essence-based skills and speech in its radius, which makes it uniquely dangerous to essence-reliant builds. Its essence is held by Ricardo Lüchenprague, leader of Orculis — one of the named Evil Spirits already active in this era.

TETRACY (Tetracea) — Floor 6, Lord of Tears. 40m+, appears in the middle of the ocean floor and floods the whole map; later phases force the fight onto open water, where losing your ship usually ends the raid on the spot.

DEAD RED — Floor 7, Lord of Darkness, one of two Lords on this floor. Its essence grants [Extinction of the Stars] — the single strongest attack skill in this system. Last summoned roughly eight years ago; near-impossible to approach without knowing the specific method.

LORD OF HOPE — Floor 8. Already killed once, inside Noark rather than Rafdonia proper.

RECARDO — Basement Floor 1, Lord of Records. Extremely rare, poorly documented even in-world; what little is known suggests power on a different scale entirely from the floor Lords above it. Tied to the deeper Record Stone mythology — treat any connection as a GM-background thread, not something a fresh character would know.

THE PATTERN. Multiple sources suggest these Lords are, in some sense, corrupted or bound followers of the Witch herself — pilgrims and collaborators from the world's oldest era, not simply "strong monsters." Worth keeping consistent if this thread ever gets pulled on directly, but not something to state as settled fact to a player.

entries.name: Bestiary — Real Weaknesses
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_STATE]
Real weaknesses and behaviors worth knowing, pulled from the full bestiary rather than invented in the moment.

Death Fiend — the actual weak point is the head; everywhere else the regeneration passive shrugs off damage. Moves slowly and won't chase past a certain range — outrunning one is a legitimate, unembarrassing option.
Banshee — will not attack first. Strike one anyway and it curses the striker with a mark of resentment, then hunts that person relentlessly until they leave the Labyrinth entirely. Most explorers who know this simply never touch one.
Vampire (base species, not the Duke) — the real weakness is solar magic and the heart specifically. Destroying the brain alone does nothing; as long as the heart survives, it comes back.
Troll — regeneration is class-defining, but a destroyed heart or head is still a clean kill regardless of how much else has healed.
Stone Golem — ranged/airflow-type attacks are disproportionately effective against it; its core, once dropped, has real material value beyond the kill itself.
Gargoyle (statue form) — inert until a target enters its sightline, at which point it petrifies and activates. Standard practice is accepting the petrification on one party member to trigger it safely rather than risking it mid-fight.
Doppelganger — becomes far harder to finish as its health drops: a defensive state near death cuts magic damage by 99% and physical by 90%. Burst it early, don't grind it down.
Tyrant Tarunbas (Glacial Cave guardian) — ice-natured despite the club, and weak specifically to lightning.
Fairy (the Rank 9 monster, not the race) — immune to physical damage entirely; magic or nothing.
Manticore — its signature ability triggers a genuinely random skill from its own kit and cannot be gained as an essence at all; treat any Manticore fight as unpredictable by design, not a gap in preparation.
Guiltigos — will never strike first unless directly provoked, but reflexively devours any other monster that comes near it, and grows stronger with every kill. Its exact strength varies wildly individual to individual for that reason.
Abyss Golem — a hard shell that shrugs off sustained fire, but the actual core inside is fragile and ends the fight the instant it's exposed.
The Native (Basement, Human Island) — see the Labyrinth entry; no wooden gear, cannot be looted normally, but can absorb essence itself.

NAMES CONFIRMED REAL, DETAIL THIN OR MISSING. Two different situations here, worth telling apart.

These three have enough real material to place properly:
Gregory the Pacifier — a Hidden Boss inside the Tower in the Sky, low-probability encounter for anyone who keeps climbing the stairs without ever branching off toward Floor 5. Historically significant: defeating him is how the Labyrinth of Larcaz was first opened, by an explorer remembered as Armella Powell Merhenia.
Berzac (Floor 6, Twin Islands) — shares a name with the Lord of the Abyss on Floor 1 but is a wholly separate entity: something recreated inside the Labyrinth from a soldier who once held high rank under Tetracy, the Lord of Tears. Attack power reads as Rank 2, but durability is Rank-1-fragile — a real glass cannon. Its true rank was never pinned down, since it mutated further under Berzac's own Abyssal Fog before anyone finished the fight.
Vulkar — genuinely unresolved even in canon between Rank 8 and Rank 9. Leave it there; don't force a pick.

Beyond those three, a real but undetailed list exists — names confirmed to occupy a specific rank, nothing else documented about them: Frahel, Leadger, Kaelnach, Mortanis, and Necramia at the upper ranks; papagonas, Bylonta, Deadleg, Astoltos, Zambet, and Mystery Gatekeeper scattered through the middle and lower ones. These are real, not placeholders — but there's nothing here to extrapolate FROM beyond the rank they were filed under. If one of these ever needs to exist on-screen, build it fresh from its rank alone, using the same grammar as everything else in this registry, and once built, keep it fixed — don't re-invent it differently a second time.

entries.name: Rafdonia — Law, Facilities, Nobility, Ghost Points
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_STATE]
FACILITIES. Motel — pay for accommodation, food included; cost varies by district (Kommelby runs roughly 9,000 stones a night). Public transport platform — a per-district wagon service, 250 stones a head, 500 for Barbarians specifically since the wagons weren't built for their size; a separate, vastly more expensive military platform exists for emergency/noble use, six times faster, roughly a million stones a ride. Ravigion Central Library — a genuinely enormous building; its sole librarian, Ragna, uses a book-detection magic that finds any specific text on request for a fee (grew from free to roughly 3,000 stones over time as staffing thinned); a restricted secret collection exists for the well-connected. Administrative agency — one per district, handles paperwork and occasionally farms out odd jobs to explorers as informal contracts. Shops — three broad types: a smithy (weapons, armor, repairs — big ones tie to specific clans), a variety store (loot resale, potions, consumables), a pub (information, party loot-splitting, usually doubles as lodging). Workshop — alchemy or magic-crafting, sells reagents and everyday magical sundries; large ones are clan-affiliated like the smithies. Alminus Central Exchange — a Kommelby institution for consignment sales and item-finding, 3,000 stones per search, with a special-appraiser service at 300,000 stones for genuinely unusual items. Alminus Bank — stores money and can be willed to a designated heir on death; a lesser-known "unregistered" deposit box exists that needs only a password, no identity — quiet, deniable storage. Tea shop and bakery — ordinary social spaces; named bakers Lubat, Nielon, and Ramus are all known in Kommelby. A church ("Daejeon") — treatment and essence erasure happen here specifically. Training ground — the one place in the city genuinely built for it: checking your own stats and matching up with prospective party members. Sky Auction House (Karnon) — high-value goods only, sealed anonymous bidding via an enchanted armrest terminal, prices kept secret until the day of. Alandsee Museum (District 9) — art and historical pieces. Public Security Agency — city policing, including drug enforcement. Royal Court — where legal judgments actually get handed down. The black market — a genuinely enormous underground space (roughly three stadiums' worth), reachable only by teleportation keyed to a magic-stone pass, with a numbered-door layout and armed security running four-to-six-floor-explorer strength; illegal even now, and slavery — nominally abolished about a century ago — still quietly happens here.

LAW. Dueling has been the one legally sanctioned form of personal violence since the earliest aristocratic era — witnessed and notarized, it doesn't count as a crime. Impersonating a noble is a capital offense. Publishing anything seriously critical of the royal family gets you exiled to Bifron for "seditious material." Treason can mean the execution of an entire family, not just the offender. Forehead branding marks a violent criminal permanently. Touching forbidden magic is itself a crime, independent of what's done with it. Barbarians are legally exempt from the usual "insulting a noble" charge that applies to every other race speaking informally to aristocracy — an old, specific, earned exception, and it doesn't extend to the king himself. Slavery was real and legal until a reform roughly a century ago abolished it outright — before that, it was a sentencing outcome, not a birthright, and most sentenced that way died anyway rather than surviving to pay their way out. In a real Labyrinth disaster, explorers are legally obligated to combine forces, which is exactly why the Labyrinth Disaster Act exists: it's the formal mechanism for settling contribution-based loot disputes after the fact, since forced cooperation reliably produces exactly that argument. Ordinary field monsters can't be claimed as "yours" unless you were genuinely within about a kilometer when they were found. During real wartime or disaster, explorers and anyone combat-capable can be legally conscripted, nobility excepted. A noble's spouse outranks them in aristocratic law if the marriage was hypogamous, and polygyny for nobles is capped by rank rather than open-ended.

NOBILITY. Over a thousand noble families exist, almost all clustered in Karnon; ordinary people are told, bluntly, to avoid them. A noble who refuses a challenged duel from a peer faces execution for it — there's no lesser outcome. Titles mostly don't get GIVEN; the standard path to nobility runs through actually distinguishing yourself as an explorer over a long career, and even then the existing aristocracy treats a self-made noble with real, often petty hostility. A titled noble can keep up to three concubines beyond a spouse; a baron specifically can hold up to three wives. Every general law bends for nobility — they answer to a separate noble code instead. Sponsoring a promising explorer is common and status-driven, closer to collecting than charity. A handful of people who were nobility or royalty somewhere else before the world ended are known to be quietly living as commoners in Rafdonia now, maintaining their own private sense of who they were without any legal standing to back it up.
Titled nobility structure: an honorary baronetcy expires with the holder; an ordinary baronet's title passes only to a son or grandson. Fewer than a hundred people in the entire city hold the rank of count. A family's noble status is formally sealed rather than simply assumed — an heir-apparent is handed an empty ceremonial box, the family crest is bound into it, and it's surrendered to the crown; that seal holds permanently, until the kingdom itself falls or the family commits outright rebellion. One real, unresolved legal tension: nobility is meant to serve only the king and kingdom, never a single race — so a tribal chief who is also personally ennobled sits in a gray area nobody has fully worked out, law or custom.

GHOST POINTS (Ghost Busters' internal currency). Bought with real information or items traded inside the network, and — unusually — rechargeable with actual outside-world money, which is exactly why using it carries real identity risk: anything routed through the real world leaves a trail. Roughly 100,000 GP converts to about 2,000,000 stones. Information itself is a tradeable good here — a trivial question pays out little, a genuinely hard one pays real GP, and some members write and sell full guides. Cosmetic-only spending exists too (chat decorations, outfits). Reputation inside the network rises with transaction volume over time and unlocks access to higher-restriction chat rooms — no other mechanical benefit — with named tiers on the way up (one documented case climbed Deadman, then Goblin & Orc, then Troll).

LAW, completion. Mozlan's own trials allow the accused to stand on silence — refusing to testify doesn't count against them the way it would in an ordinary court. A generation ago, official policy quietly tolerated minors entering the Labyrinth despite the letter of the law forbidding it; the law itself hasn't changed, enforcement has. Military law runs on strict succession — if a superior officer dies or is incapacitated mid-command, the next-ranking officer takes over automatically, no debate. Under the Labyrinth Law specifically, an explorer's own knowledge and experience cannot be legally compelled out of them — no one can force what you know, only what you do. Marriage between two noble houses never actually merges them into one family under the law, whatever the personal relationship becomes. Direct collaboration with the aristocracy is itself restricted by law for non-nobles — sponsorship and service exist, but formal partnership does not.

NAMED HOUSES, confirmed real and fixed — once introduced, stay consistent with these, don't invent contradictory versions:
Marquis of Tercerion — family emblem a shield with a thorn tree. For decades, while the king rarely appeared in public, Tercerion handled most of his official duties in his place. The kingdom's second-in-command family, answering to no one but the crown itself.
Duke Kealunus — one of the old Great Families, tracing back to the Mada Pagoda bloodline. Actively invested in Labyrinth-related business specifically, with real, strong influence over the large clans.
Countess of Alminus — not an old family; it wasn't present at Rafdonia's founding. Its power is newer and more commercial: it owns the Alminus Central Exchange and Alminus Bank outright — the same facilities already documented in Civic Life. When either comes up, the Countess is their real owner, not an anonymous institution. A supporter of the cog-teeth clan, and through that connection has real reach into Labyrinth affairs despite the family's youth.
Melves — an alliance of 32 noble families across different races, not one house. Every member family but the Barbarians has a real connection to the royal family and shares information across tribal lines; all of them have some tie to a sacred site kept deliberately behind the scenes. Two real structural weaknesses: the aristocracy at large ostracizes and watches them for being multiracial, and the highest title any Melves house can hold is count, a hard ceiling. It is genuinely notable, not incidental, that Bjorn Yandel became the first person outside Melves in 600 years to gain the right to attend a royal meeting because of them.
Federation of Small and Medium Nobles — the collective political voice of the lesser houses, distinct from the great families above.
Count Lumina, Count Bolsche — named members of the mid-tier nobility.
Viscount Verton — the house has a real, recent succession story: the Viscount died during the Noark invasion, leaving only a disabled infant heir, and a collateral relative used the opening to usurp the viscountcy outright. That's the current holder's real, known origin, not just a title.

MOZLAN, additional confirmed detail beyond what's already established: offices exist scattered across the city, with the real headquarters in Karnon itself. They flatly do not deal with anyone who isn't aristocracy — bribes don't move them, common petitioners get nothing. Notably, this held true even inside the original Dungeon & Stone video game — Mozlan read as closed-minded and unhelpful there too, a rare case of the real world and the game agreeing on an NPC faction's personality. Investigating the Magic Tower's wizards specifically, in cases touching aristocratic assassination, falls under Mozlan's authority rather than anyone else's.

THESE HOUSES ARE REACHABLE, NOT JUST BACKGROUND. Bjorn Yandel is proof of the ceiling — a tournament guest, eventually the first Barbarian-born baron in the kingdom's history, the first outsider admitted to a royal meeting in 600 years of Melveth history. None of that happened from fame alone; it happened because real feats connected to real houses for real reasons. See noble-contacts for how this actually triggers in play — it's a genuine, earnable path, not scenery the player can only read about.

entries.name: Economy & the Tax
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_LAW]
TWO THINGS CALLED STONES. Get this right.

MANA STONES are physical: gravel cut out of a monster corpse, graded by the rank of what died. They are loot. They buy nothing anywhere in Rafdonia.

STONES are the currency: stamped coin and Guild credit, what every price in this world is quoted in. Everyone calls it "stones" because the whole economy is backed by processed mana stones — Rafdonia's alchemists transmute them into wheat, clay, iron ore, mythril. The stones are simultaneously the money supply and the food supply. That is why the city cannot let the Labyrinth close.

THE CONVERSION: an Explorers' Guild exchange counter on the surface grades the haul by rank, weighs it, records it, handles the city's tax deduction, and pays out coin minus the Guild's cut. That is the ONLY conversion point.

THE ANCHOR: one Rank 9 mana stone exchanges for exactly 20 stones, which buys one loaf of bread. A Death Fiend's (Rank 8) exchanges for 100. Every price below scales off those two numbers.

THE TAX. Owed from age twenty, by every resident, to live inside the walls. Failure to pay is punishable by death; lesser failure states include demotion to lower-class citizen status. Confirmed figures from Chapter 18, for a non-human: 700,000 stones for the first year, 800,000 from the second year onward, plus exchange fees after the initial exemption period. Bjorn recalls the Dungeon & Stone version being 600,000 — the real world is NOT numerically identical to the game, and {{user}}'s memorized figures will be subtly wrong in ways that cost them.

DO THE ARITHMETIC AND LET IT LAND: 700,000 stones is thirty-five thousand Goblin mana stones, or seven thousand Death Fiends. Retail hunting does not pay the tax. That is the design, not bad luck.

Tax burden varies by race and status. Draconians pay nothing. Elves, Dwarves and Beastmen have institutional arrangements and access to tax-loan financing. BARBARIANS AND HUMANS HAVE NO TAX-LOAN POLICY — no safety net, no deferral, nothing between them and the deadline.

PRICE ANCHORS for consistency: a loaf of bread 20 stones. A Kommelby motel night ~9,000. District wagon 250, or 500 for a Barbarian. A library search ~3,000. Castaway's Ring of Vigor 2,000,000. Guardian's Wrist Guard ~50,000,000. Bjorn's Immortality Imprint started at 550,000 stones for Stage 1 and doubled per stage into the millions. Essences are worth more than gold to an explorer purely because the odds of getting one are so bad.

OTHER MONEY: information is sold through Guild channels. Loans exist and are predatory. Plunderers are a real profession — explorers who rob other explorers of gear, because equipment out-earns mana-stone hunting for a skilled enough predator. And a heavy pouch walking through Ravigion toward a counter is the most robbed thing in the city.

entries.name: The Labyrinth — Floors, Rifts, Hidden Fields
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_LAW]
CORE RULES. Opens midnight, 1st of every month, through the Dimensional Squares in every Ravigion district. Entry position inside is random. The only way out is waiting for a floor's own close-date — it "spits out" everyone still inside. Floors 1-5 reset fully each new cycle; floor 6 onward does not (see Floor 6). Confirmed close-times, all seven floors: Floor 1 — 168 hours (7 days). Floor 2 — 240 hours (10 days). Floor 3 — 15 days. Floor 4 — 23 days. Floor 5 — 30 days. Floor 6 — 60 days. Floor 7 — 75 days. Duration climbs steadily with depth.

TIME. Whatever the trip's actual length inside — hours or subjective weeks — the surface only ever sees the player return around midday the day after they went down. Character age and wear track the LONGER, subjective clock instead (see labyrinth-days). A three-day hunt and a three-week one both cost the surface exactly one calendar day, but only one of those wears the same amount off a person.

FLOOR NUMBER IS NOT MONSTER RANK. Every floor below has its native band, but rare spawns, rift guardians, hidden bosses, and unlisted mutant variants can appear well outside it, on any floor, at any time.

— FLOOR 1: CRYSTAL CAVE —
Self-lit by wall crystals; no torch needed except one dark patch. Four portals, one per compass direction, each with its own dominant monster: east Blade Wolf, west Gnome, south Ghoul, north Goblin (this exact mapping has drifted across canon tellings — treat it as the current baseline, not gospel). Center: a ~30m safe cavity holding a monument to a legendary "Great Sage." Terrain reshuffles every cycle around a few fixed landmarks. Rank 9: Goblin, Ghoul, Gnome, Blade Wolf. During a major world-event ("Berzak" active), Rank 5 Abyssal variants of all four replace them. Rifts: Bloody Citadel, Glacial Cave, Green Coal Mine, Steel Tomb.

— FLOOR 2 (closes day 10): four regions, four portals from Floor 1 —
Beast's Den (east) — canyon maze, brutal to navigate without tracking/scent abilities. Rank 9: Mighty Razor Wolf, Wall Mole Queen. Rank 8: Saber Tiger, Werewolf.
Land of the Dead (south) — black mud, narrow visibility, banshee cries at a distance. Easiest route to Floor 3, no traps, just dark. Rank 9: Ghoul, Elder Ghoul, Skeleton (+Warrior/Archer/Mage variants), Banshee. Rank 8: Death Fiend, Chimera Wolf, Ghoul Lord. Rank 7: Dullahan. Rank 6: Death Knight.
Rocky Desert (west) — sand and heat, gnome mutants, kobolds hunt in trios. Rank 9: Gnome, Kobold, Kobold Shieldman. Rank 8: Stone Golem, Sandman, Sandworm.
Goblin Forest (north) — starlit visibility, heavily trapped, goblin-dominant. Eight portal monuments; opening one turns the rest to stone, so latecomers must search from scratch (avg. 2-3 days alone). Rank 9: Goblin, Goblin Swordsman, Goblin Archer. Rank 7: Hobgoblin.

— FLOOR 3: PILGRIM'S PATH — a wide layer, ten-plus named fields around a central forest.
Ironrock Hill — highland start (Beast's Den route), overlooks the whole floor. On day 3 of a cycle, silver light rises to the ceiling for one minute — cause unconfirmed even in-world. Rank 8: Wormstone, Iron Falcon, Ironhill Guardian. Rank 7: Aiantro — this may or may not be the same entity as "Ilatrek," a separately-documented Rank 7 with an active called [Blitz]; the two sources don't confirm they're identical, so treat them as two distinct possibilities rather than force a merge.
Orc Colony — densest monster population on the floor, rank 8-and-up only, second-hardest area here. Rank 8: Orc Shaman, Orc Warrior, Orc Archer. Rank 7: Orc Champion. Hidden bosses via altar sacrifice: the Orc Heroes (Rank 5) or, rarely, an Orc Lord (Rank 2) instead.
Twilight Slope / Blackfish / Greentail Marsh — start points for the Rocky Desert, Land of the Dead, and Goblin Forest routes respectively. Blackfish: branching drainage ditches, Rank 8 Frogman. Greentail: Rank 8 Lizardman Scout.
Sculpture Temple — ruined stone buildings, statues with broken necks, one dominant monster: Rank 7 Nameless Statue.
Thorn Reed Field — flat, shoulder-high reeds, bordering the Witch's Forest.
Witch's Forest (center, surrounds the Floor 4 portal) — half its monsters are physically immune, magic or mental attacks only. Compass useless; even the trees seem to move. Entering applies escalating debuffs: [confusion], double [hallucination], [pain amplified]. After 12 hours the field debuff [Witch's Eye] begins, worsening over 84 hours through five stages; each stage shortens how long you can safely stay in one spot before a Kanivaro spawns to punish you — roughly an hour on day one, ten minutes by day three, three minutes at the worst stage. Rank 9: Fairy, Wraith, Witch's Lamp, Woodman. Rank 8: Owl Bear, Dryad, Homunculus, Snetree, Dairouter, Mutant Low-Rank Spirit. Rank 7: Half-Troll, Carnivaro. A safe zone, the Witch's Hut, spawns randomly and lasts 8 hours, up to five people, found by resting a hand on a bark that glows purple; sacrificing a corpse on its hearth extends it another 8 hours.

— FLOOR 4 (closes day 23): TOWER IN THE SKY — the entry portal from Floor 3 visibly changes color when it's safe to enter; going through outside that window risks being mistaken for a plunderer by whoever's already inside, with real attack consequences, not just a social faux pas. This is a genuine coordination signal, not flavor — a staged trial tower, independent structure. Entry: a stone room, locked doors on every wall, monsters pour in as the first trial (grouped like Floor 3's habitats). Clearing opens the doors — Courage, Wisdom, Patience, Destiny — pick one stair per stage:
Courage — random fight, 4-hour cooldown before the next stage. ~16 days to reach stage 100 via this path alone — too slow to reach Floor 5 before the cycle closes if it's the only route taken.
Wisdom — a shortcut climbing five stages at once, but the road is trapped and the fights are real; no cooldown between choices.
Patience — a psychological ordeal, hallucinated past hurts. Reward: a box that can yield a Numbered Item or a random Rank 6-or-lower essence.
Destiny — rare (<5% appearance), unpredictable; one of roughly 32 special trial types (a fight back to Floor 1's danger level, a straight Rank 5 monster, a secret-room trap). Best rewards on the tower. Landing on Destiny three separate times unlocks entry to this floor's hidden fields.
Difficulty caps and holds at stage 100 — Rank 6 becomes common, Rank 5 a real (if rare) possibility from here on. The Floor 5 portal is only searchable from stage 100+, and needs the right door sequence to find. No monster respawns once a stage is cleared.

— FLOOR 5 (closes day 30): GREAT DEMON REALM — open-world canyon maze, clan-scale hunting is normal here. Branching "slide" terrain with broken, rope-crossed gaps.
Start Point — safe camp zone.
Hellfire Canyon — [Hellfire Gorge] field effect: all resource consumption ×1.5, fire resistance −30. Rank 8: Dead of Fire. Rank 7: Millarodden (rare), Red Mud. Rank 6: Stoneburn. Rank 5: Ifrit, Hell Flame.
Frost Canyon — essences here specifically synergize with cold-attribute builds.
Wraith's Canyon — closest route to Floor 6. [Gorge of Ghosts] field effect: periodic ground tremors, dark and physical resistance −100. Rank 8: Corrupted Creature. Rank 6: Curse Stone. Rank 5: Bloodshot Ghost, Soul Eater.

— FLOOR 6: THE GREAT OCEAN — the one floor that does NOT reset each cycle; it runs its own continuous clock. Real sky, real sun, white sand on arrival. Requires a boat — from here on, a dedicated navigator role and clan-scale investment are the norm. "Grand Rock," a region of rock and volcanic islands, covers ~99% of the map; three specific red rock islands regenerate randomly each cycle.
Laemia (Island of Beginning) — universal starting point; grows a wood as hard as Rank 3 metal and light enough to float. Build your boat here.
Farune Island — west, insect-monster hunting (Rank 8 and under). Destroying its central tribute triggers an island-wide defense event that scales with party size. Rank 5: Siren. Rank 4: Siren Queen, Guano Sea Serpent. Rank 3: Storm Gush.
Anos Island — jungle terrain. Rank 7: Raffle Monkey. Rank 5: Belgaro.
Pione Island ("Treasure Island") — the only non-Rift source of Numbered Items in the game. Rank 4 Lapremimic monsters guarantee a Numbered Item on a kill; an essence here can be worth billions of stones.
Katakoma ("Skull Island") — hidden-boss access toward Floor 10 content. Locally elevated difficulty (Rank 6-8 despite a nominal average of 6). Rank 4: Keykeeper. Rank 3: Skeleton King (variant).
Arta Island — closest to Katakoma, no monsters, three unexplained pillar structures (one of the Seven Wonders of the Labyrinth), and a hidden entrance to Arta's own base.
Minor islands, sparse detail: Gurkha (low-tier, near start), Ghost Island, Pirate Islands (SW, orc/goblin raiders), Serene Fairy Island, Golem Island, Stannells Island (a lone unexplained monument), Dark Cloud Island.

— FLOOR 7 (closes day 75) — two disconnected regions reached separately from Floor 6, both leading on to Floor 8: the Dark Continent and a second, colder region. Confirmed Dark Continent locale: Ghost's Canyon. Ruins here ("Pantlion") connect to the hidden 7th Archive — see Basement, Rainbow Island.

— FLOOR 8: LAND OF THE DAWN — first arrival grants +50 soul power outright. A narrow green garden, the smallest field area of any floor, and genuinely safe — no ambient monsters. Instead exactly one crack is always open, type randomized. Clearing it opens two portals: on to Floor 9, or loop back into a freshly regenerated Floor 8. Repeats indefinitely. Confirmed rift here: Calhaem, City of Light, guarded by the Celestial Spearman Milayel, a Rank 2 entity — the same one whose essence and Numbered Item No. 7 (Milayel's Verdurous Giant Spear) are already documented. A second confirmed rift, Red Dragon's Heart, is guarded by an actual Rank 1 dragon.

— FLOOR 9: STAR'S END — a recurring field event: a meteor strike lights a ~50m warning radius; the inner 5m is instant death, the outer ring deals damage heavy enough to one-shot most tanks. After impact, lightning strikes the crater and spawns a Rank 2 Gigazeros.
Primeval Land (center) — under specific conditions, an ancient dragon can be summoned here.
Old Rock Meadow (west) — a spirit door; Rank 3 Bayon present.
Poisonous Lava Field (north). Dreamy Waterfall (east) — the hardest ground on this floor. Yongol Mountain (south).

— FLOOR 10 — the Gate of the Abyss. Requires all six Genesis Treasures. Entry is capped near one full party. Near the end, a puzzle-like sequence must be solved in the correct order — failure risks wiping the whole party — and the approach to the Gate itself is scattered with instant-death trap tiles.

— BASEMENT, FLOOR 1: THE ARCHIVE — entrance is a single monument in a ~10m passage, opened with three "nameless pieces." No natural exit: like a Rift, it admits people then seals — but unlike a Rift, the entry point is fixed and permanent, not roaming. The portal in also shuts once 60 people have entered in one opening. You have to find your own way out.
The "Sea of Records" is a silver, mercury-like ocean; things lost from the rest of the Labyrinth wash up in it.
RAINY SEASON: on days 14-21 of this level's own 30-day inner cycle, monsters fall from the sky and hiding is the only real option; the level's total cycle runs 50 days before resetting, offset from the surface's own calendar.
Rock Island — starting point, barren, nothing here at all.
Human Island ("Monster Island") — home to the Native: big-eyed, blue-skinned, ~3m tall, calling themselves "human," speaking their own ancient language, living in stone-built villages lit by a natural glow, working metal without fire. Not hostile by default; a real, distinct culture, not a monster-spawn zone. Mechanically unusual if it ever comes to violence: a Native cannot be looted the normal way — no guaranteed drop, no Numbered Item eligibility — but it CAN absorb essence itself, caps somewhere between 3 and 7 depending on the individual, and its passive turns anything wooden to dust on contact, gloves included. Bring nothing wooden.
Tree Island — roughly a day's sail out; a climbing dungeon inside a single colossal tree.
Island of Giants — ~10x Human Island's size; every monster here can use Gigantization. Shelter from the rainy season exists on its south coast. A 40m+ "super giant" is rumored as its unconfirmed final boss. Rank 8: Werewolf. Rank 5: Troll.
Seokmun ("Stone Gate") Island — a hallway of guardian statues: 27 identified Rift Guardians spanning Floors 1-5, plus 14 unidentified ones. Touching a statue opens a solo fight (up to Floor 4's guardian) or a two-person fight (Floor 5's); buffs are stripped on entry, and a win guarantees an essence but never a Rift Stone or Numbered Item. Clearing every Floor-5-or-lower statue opens the door to the Third Archive, a deeper crack.
Rainbow Island — appears only in a brief window, then vanishes; standing there at the right moment transports to the Pantlion Ruins on Floor 7's Dark Continent — a hidden factory (the "7th Archive") that converts magic stones into monsters and back, and permits crafting a genuine custom essence from three hybrid monster components.
Library Island — a two-cylinder temple, one entrance, 200+ stairs down to a cylindrical archive. Each book documents a monster with real numeric stats (not the vague high/medium/low banding used everywhere else) and its essence colors in detail. Placing a book on the central slab summons that monster to fight; a monster must first be discovered for real, in the world, before its book becomes usable this way. Considered one of the best controlled hunting grounds in the Labyrinth for exactly that reason — you choose the pace.

— RIFTS (every floor) — reopen on a real cooldown: minimum two cycles, typically somewhere between the fourth and fifth, guaranteed reopened by the eighth. This is now engine-resolved, not a GM call — see rift-state, rolled fresh by real dice every time a new cycle begins. A rift also needs at least three real days to generate naturally, reflected as accessibleFromDay in that state. First party to reach an open rift gets first crack at the guardian. Contested drops (a Numbered Item, Rift Stone, or essence more than one party wants) are settled by a straight high-roll dice contest between claimants — not combat. Confirmed rifts by floor: F1 — Bloody Citadel, Glacial Cave, Green Coal Mine, Steel Tomb. F2 — Gunpo/Rocky Desert. F3 — White Temple. F4 — Doppelganger Forest. F5 — Fortress of the Soul, Island of Paradise. F7 — Balantis. F8 — Calhaem, City of Light and Red Dragon's Heart. Basement — Third Archive. Mutant rifts (an off-roster or unusually powerful guardian in an ordinary-looking rift) exist at extremely low probability.

— HIDDEN FIELDS — distinct from Rifts: no guardian, standard drop rates, but high difficulty and correspondingly high reward. Share their host floor's close-date.
Labyrinth of Larcaz (Floor 4) — maze under [Guardian of Balance]: total party stats redistribute equally, which specifically benefits wizards, since they can't otherwise use essence at all. Random mid-boss rooms, then a final boss room (a mutated Minotaur, "Rakzar") guarding the run's headline reward.
Mirror of Fire (Floor 5) — teleports into an open-world extension. [Underworld] field effect boosts mana-stone drop rate and lightly boosts essence drop; compass disabled; only one looted item can be carried back out per visit; monsters take a full day to respawn, making the field briefly safe after a clear. Rank 5 Berthas appears here, rarely, in its Burning Forest sub-area.
Atlante (Floor 6) — a sunken temple; needs a boat, diving capability, and patience to find. [Atlante] field effect eventually doubles all resource consumption. A giant blue egg at its center is guarded by Deep Sea Giants; witnessing it is itself an achievement.
"End" (Floor 6, via Katakoma) — a 24-hour fire-damage field that cannot be re-entered once left. Leads to Arta's hidden base (blood-altar entry) and a raid against the Rank 1 boss Snictura, fought under special rules with soul power sealed for everyone involved.
Eternal Hall (Floor 9) — entered through a "Gate of Spirit"; four elemental sub-fields, each held by a Rank 1 Primal Spirit. Doubles as a fast-travel hub: it can teleport a party to anywhere they've already legitimately explored below Floor 9, including the closed Basement, and offers real-time visibility into what's currently happening elsewhere in the Labyrinth.
Hell — a punitive field some misused Numbered Items can drag a wearer into. Effectively unsurvivable; there is no confirmed way back.
Home — resembles the Mirror of Fire but reconstructs specific historical figures instead of monsters. Explicitly not worth entering except during a Dimensional Collapse.

LABYRINTH EXPEDITION / RE-ENTRY LAW — HARD CANON BEHAVIOR.
- The ordinary Rafdonia entrance opens at midnight on the 1st of the monthly cycle. An explorer does NOT treat the Labyrinth like a dungeon they can surface from and re-enter every day.
- Once an explorer enters for that cycle, their expedition continues inside until the Labyrinth/floor returns them to the city according to its portal/closure mechanics. Returning to Rafdonia ends that cycle's expedition; ordinary re-entry waits for the next opening cycle unless a specific canon exception explicitly applies.
- Floor closure clocks are LABYRINTH-ELAPSED time: Floor 1 = 168 hours / 7 days; Floor 2 = 240 hours / 10 days; Floor 3 = 15 days; Floor 4 = UNKNOWN / NOT HARD-CODED; Floor 5 = 30 days; Floor 6 = 60 days; Floor 7 = 75 days.
- Labyrinth elapsed time and Rafdonia surface calendar time are distinct. Preserve the existing time-dilation rule in this world: however long the expedition is lived inside, ordinary return advances the surface cycle by exactly one day from the descent day and emerges around midday. The explorer's body, supplies, fatigue, wounds, hunger, thirst, sleep, and lived experience track the longer Labyrinth clock.
- Do not invent a universal numeric 'Labyrinth day = X Rafdonia hours' conversion beyond the established return behavior. Treat the two clocks as separate domains.
- A party may divide loot, rations, mana stones, watches, or provisional shares while inside. But contracts must not casually promise 'daily payment when we surface,' 'surface every night,' 'come back tomorrow and re-enter,' or any other repeated surface/re-entry loop.
- Recruitment dialogue and party contracts should normally describe payment as an expedition share, a split of the haul/proceeds upon return to Rafdonia, an upfront retainer plus return settlement, or another physically/canonically plausible arrangement.

MONTHLY RAFDONIA ENTRY WINDOW — SIMULATION CLOCK VALUE: The ordinary Rafdonia Labyrinth entrance opens at 00:00 (midnight) on surface Day 1. For this simulation, close ordinary entry at approximately 01:00, giving a one-hour entry window. Canon explicitly supports midnight opening, that the gate remains open at least 40 minutes later, and a final 10/5/1-minute countdown with the portal shrinking; the exact 01:00 closing timestamp is a STRONG INFERENCE adopted as the runtime value, not an explicitly stated canon timestamp. Therefore: 00:00 open; ~00:50 final 10-minute phase; ~00:55 final 5-minute phase; ~00:59 final minute; ~01:00 closed. Do not confuse this monthly ENTRY closure with a floor's expedition closure/expulsion clock.
RIFT PORTAL TEN-MINUTE RULE — CANON, CONTEXT-SPECIFIC: For the statue-activated guardian portals investigated by Bjorn in the later special stone-chamber sequence, an opened portal closes after 10 minutes IF NOBODY ENTERS. Once a person enters, portal behavior follows that portal's capacity/type; the observed lower guardian portals were single-person and disappeared after the entrant, while the highest-difficulty fifth-floor guardian statue produced two portals/two-person capacity. Do NOT turn the 10-minute inactivity rule into a universal law for every rift or portal in the Labyrinth: ordinary rifts have multiple portal behaviors, including portals that persist until their designated number of entrants passes and one-time-use portals. Use the 10-minute no-entry expiry only where that statue/guardian portal rule or an explicitly equivalent canon rule applies.

AUTHORITY CONTRACT: Explicit entrance/floor/return/rift mechanics in this entry are CANON LAW unless a sentence is specifically labeled inference. Descriptive appearance and atmosphere remain CANON REFERENCE.

entries.name: Bestiary Registry
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_REFERENCE]
Ranks run 9 (weakest) to 1 (apex), plus Unranked. Floor number does NOT equal monster rank — rare spawns, rift guardians, hidden bosses and Lords of the Floor can produce threats far above the local band.

UNRANKED: Deadman, Skull Rat. These give no mana stones and no EXP, and their corpses do not vanish on death unless they drop an essence.

RANK 9: Banshee, Blade Wolf, Bloody Blade Wolf, Corrupted Gnome, Deep Salmon, Elder Ghoul, Fairy, Frost Wolf, Ghoul, Giant Blade Wolf, Goblin, Goblin Archer, Goblin Swordsman, Gnome, Iron Golem, Kobold Shield Soldier, Moon Rock Bear, Mummy, Queen Wall Mole, Skeleton, Skeleton Archer, Skeleton Warrior, Slime, Spectre, Sterrap, Wall-Mole Rat, Watcher of the Abyss, Witch's Lamp, Woodman, Wraith.

RANK 8: Ancient Spider, Chimera Wolf, Corrupted Creature, Dairouter, Dead of Fire, Death Fiend, Dryad, Frogman, Frogman Shaman, Gargoyle, Ghoul Lord, Gremlin, Homunculus, Ice Golem, Iron Falcon, Ironrock Hill Guardian Soldier, Lizardman Scout, Megalith Soldier, Mutant Low-Rank Spirit, Orc Archer, Orc Sorcerer, Orc Warrior, Owl Bear, Saber Tiger, Sandman, Snetree, Stone Golem, Werewolf, Wormstone.

RANK 7: Bone Knight, Canyon Ghost, Carnivaro, Conch Horn, Corpse Golem, Dark Worshipper, Deadburn, Dullahan, Half-Troll, Headhunter, Ice Orc Sorcerer, Ice Orc Warrior, Ilatrek, Iron Tusk, Katoomba, Mighty Orc Warrior, Millarodden, Mimic, Queen Banshee, Ranemut Warrior, Red Mud, Tyrant Tarunbas, Vitol, Yeti.

RANK 6: Curse Stone, Death Knight, Dragoon, Gachabon, Ghosties, Hell Guard, Hell Hound, Red Eye, Salamander, Stoneburn, Teeth Skeleton, Vaikundus.

RANK 5: Abyssal Blade Wolf, Abyssal Goblin, Argos, Baphomet, Berthas, Bloodshot Ghost, Culves, Dakirion, Death Worm, Doom Warrior, Drake, Duocorn, Hell Flame, Ifrit, Knight of the End, Malder Elephant, Manticore, Minotaur, Orc Hero, Redwood, Soul Eater, Troll, Vampire Duke Cambormere.

RANK 4: Banshee Queen, Chaosseaman, Doppelganger, Guano Sea Serpent, Lich, Nightmare, Katanda, Sea Merchant, Siren Queen, Soul Drinker, Soul Colossus, Steel Giant.

RANK 3: Bayon, Bellarios, Deep Sea Giant, Nibaroque, Ogre, Spear Dipper, Storm Gush, Vandemon, Vol-Herchan.

RANK 2: BrainStep, Extreme Thunder, Gigazeros, Hypramagent, Man-Faced Bird, Thundercloud, Titanus.

RANK 1: Bone Dragon, Cryptid, Dryzen, Guiltygos, Kashan, Leviathan, Plahel, Ridger, Snikutra, Taurbrood, Tol-Lapupa.

NOTABLE BEHAVIOR: Goblins use small double-headed axes and daggers. Goblin Archers use harp-shaped wooden bows, poison their arrowheads, and know Thief Step, a stealth magic most effective while still or moving slowly. Elder Ghouls are twice normal size, enjoy tormenting prey, and are classed as no-first-strike — they do not initiate. Death Fiends regenerate almost instantly from non-lethal wounds via Body Preservation, summon Ghouls with Call of the Dead, and cannot get back up once knocked down. Dryads disguise themselves as attractive people pulled from the target's own memories. Bayons are humans with a black parasitic spider fused to the face, each with unique abilities drawn from other monsters' essences — likely the reanimated remains of explorers who died down there. Berthas looks Rank 3 and is Rank 5; Bjorn considers it the monster whose power most exceeds its appearance.

entries.name: Numbered Items Registry
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_LAW]
FINITE NUMBERING RULE: Numbered Items occupy a unique 1-10,000 numbering namespace. This does NOT mean 10,000 JSON objects exist. Only canon-known or legitimately discovered items are instantiated. An unknown number remains an empty/unknown slot until the world actually surfaces it. No two physical Numbered Items may share a number. Use the numbered-item-ledger variable as the ownership authority. Lower numbers generally correlate with prestige/power, but not linearly.

Numbered Items drop from Rift Guardians (one of three loot types), are found far behind the scenes, or surface from ancient holdings. Twelve of them are talismans, and an explorer may use only ONE talisman at a time. Lower numbers strongly correlate with prestige and power, but the correlation is not linear — some four-digit items are strategically transformative and some low numbers are niche.

CONFIRMED REGISTRY (number — name — holder — effect):
9999 Beginner's Luck, Ainar Fenelin. Soulbound on first touch, never transferable. +5 percentage points to essence drop, FIRST-TIME kills only: 0.01% becomes 5.01%, 33% becomes 38%. Additive, not multiplicative.
9981 Castaway's Ring of Vigor. Valued 2,000,000 stones.
9712 Snow Field Club. Adds cold treatment on top of normal damage.
9425 Ring of the Frost Spirit, Missha Karlstein. Seals one absorbed essence's abilities (not its stats); drops only in rifts below the third floor; if destroyed, triggers a special effect for a Beastman without a contract, freeing the Skadia Glacial Beast.
8820 Iron Wall, Bjorn Yandel. Doubles physical and mana resistance for 3 seconds.
8667 Outlaw of the Wilderness, Bjorn Yandel. Close-combat bonus vs humanoids, scaling with their number. Long cooldown.
8645 Purification Torch, Sawtooth Clan. Raid utility for Riakis phase mechanics.
7777 Garpha's Necklace, formerly Bjorn Yandel. Consumes magic stones to produce random goods — can yield other Numbered Items.
7612 Pride of the Necromancer. Pairs with 7611; adds blood recovery.
7611 Deceit of the Necromancer, Abman Urikfried. Fatal-damage failsafe: suspended animation plus temporary immunity. Breaks after three uses.
7234 Misplaced Trust, Arua Raven / Bjorn Yandel. Creates a roughly 10m zone where lying is impossible.
6111 Destiny Seeker, Regal Vagos / Bjorn Yandel. Color indicator for nearby positive, negative, or mixed events.
5991 Serpent's Fang, Missha Karlstein / Jencia Nephrin. Large penetration bonus; doubles poison damage through the sword.
4819 Lava Shield. High-level shield loaned through wizards for anti-fire preparation.
3120 Second Heart, Regal Vagos. Consumable protection after instant-death damage to the heart.
3112 Guardian's Wrist Guard, Hikurod Murad. ~50,000,000 stones. One-use knockdown plus temporary ally status immunity.
2998 Mark of the Guardians, Bjorn Yandel. Earring; with a shield equipped, absorbs 50% of impacts.
2578 Sky Armor, Jaina Flyer. High-end defensive item.
1911 Fabler's Broken Pocket Watch, Titana Akurava. Removes cooldowns entirely for dwarves for 5 minutes; 70% reduction for other races.
1577 Coffin of Eternal Rest, Baekho Lee. Improves physical recovery; durable sealed sleeping container.
1001 Alonso's Travel Bag, Auyen Rockrobe. Soulbound talisman; lowers threat ~40%, increases mana-stone drop rate 1.5x.
989 Orb of Circulation, Versyl Gowland. Greatly improves natural regeneration outside critical condition.
981 Firefly Ring, Bjorn Yandel. Glows near Gabrielius arrangements and hidden pieces.
777 Macairo's Storage Box, Yurven Havellion. Consumable random reward or permanent buff; can dud. Yielded the secret Dragon Plate of Aegis.
761 Loam's Blast Furnace Hammer, Melend Kaislan. Fire-penetration damage proportional to physical strength.
760 Fire Dragon Ring. Wizard-loaned anti-fire item.
696 Imperial Bow of Raindres, Erwen Fornacci di Tersia.
687 Siege Slaughterer, Bjorn Yandel. Extremely high-damage mace; +40% strength, -80% agility.
666 Hans Ferret's Outing Doll, Bjorn Yandel. Remote doll / alt-character; the doll can level and absorb essences independently.
535 Polar Region Shield. High-tier shield, notable for Shield Barbarian builds.
444 Dedrius' Invitation. Undead do not attack the holder; breaking the seal sends the user to the special zone Hell.
399 Cage of Silence. Trap reacting to transport abilities; seals magic, divine power and aura within its radius.
87 Kraul's Demon Grinder, Bjorn Yandel. Major blunt-skill multiplier, reduced soul-energy cost, knockdown penetration.
35 Rake of Naraka. Paired claw weapon, multiple effects.
21 Unknown graduation shield. No information exists.
19 Exenith Demon Dragon Sword, Ravien. Transmutation longsword; amplifies physical damage and can convert it to magical.
18 Rift Maker. Consumes rift stones to open a real rift on the current floor.
17 Staff of the Netherworld, Abed Necrapeto. Sends user and target to an Underworld field with undead/living stat rules.
16 Ebony Insignia, Amelia Rainwales / Golden Tree Clan. Absolute stealth while stationary; can distribute temporary stealth tokens.
12 Trust. Multi-person soul-linked bracelet, permanent binding, role-flexible: Tank takes no damage from bonded allies; Dealer's damage scales with number bonded; Priest's beneficial effects on bonded allies double.
7 Milayel's Verdurous Giant Spear, Ainar Fenelin. Apex spear — huge penetration, sustain, immunity and resource-refund effects.
3 Wall of Aegis, Bjorn Yandel. Indestructible tower shield, the strongest known.
UNNUMBERED SECRETS: Flower Crown of Despair (nullifies mental attacks but also divine power and healing), Dragon Plate of Aegis (soulbound Aegis set armor), Banner of the Sun (Lord Dzarwi Clan), Lukberta's Pigeon Boots (Guold Aldidi, speed for Soul Power). Item No. 1 or 2 belongs to the Royal Family; function unknown.

METALS, used to craft or destroy them: Iron is baseline. Moonstone is grade 4, high durability. Adamantium and Idium are grade 5. Arc and Mystium are grade 6 — the most perfected materials in Rafdonia, and capable of destroying most any Numbered Item.

RESONANT NOBLE PHANTASMS — set items with a real bonus once both pieces are held together, confirmed real, not flavor. Necromancer Set (No. 7611 + No. 7612): when either piece's effect activates, an additional 50% of the blood spent is recovered. This one is interface-enforced — the moment both numbers are actually held, the bonus is live and the GM gets told directly, so it should never need to be remembered by hand. Aegis Set (No. 3, Aegis Wall + the Secret Number Aegis's Dragon Armor): increases all regeneration speed, not just one resource — natural regeneration rises too. This one can't be interface-detected the same way, since its second piece is an unrevealed Secret Number the system has no way to recognize by number alone — the GM has to track this one by hand, but it is exactly as real as the Necromancer Set once both pieces are confirmed present. Don't let the lack of a UI checkmark make it feel optional.

entries.name: The Six Races — Full
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: CANON_LAW]
Heterogeneous races together make up just over 1% of the population — humans are the overwhelming majority. Every non-Draconian race pays several times more tax than humans do. Barbarians alone have no legal option but the Labyrinth; every other race can hold a day job in the city on top of, or instead of, exploring.

— HUMAN — average height 170cm. The largest share of explorers simply because they're the largest share of everyone. Career paths: Aura user (see below), spiritist, wizard, priest. A rare few are born barbarian-sized, but that's the exception, not a racial trait. No innate ability at all — the tradeoff is that nothing closes to them. Human children raised near a temple learn to read and reason from a young age, which is why late-game human potential runs unusually high; the title of "priest" carries real social weight here for the same reason. Tax is meaningfully lower than every other race but Draconians and clergy. Marriage and childbirth are the socially correct path, and having a child reduces tax for 20 years.
AUROR — Human-exclusive. Requires a sword specifically, since a blade is what channels it best. Drawing on mana wreathes the blade in an aura, color varies by person. Effect: ignores 90% of defense and 90% of magic resistance — functionally cheating. Lets a wielder infuse the tip for a short-range instant close. Only about one in a hundred people who could theoretically learn it actually can. A Rank-5-equivalent "ordinary knight" who can manifest an aura is considered on par with a Floor-6 explorer, and outranks one in a direct duel. Skill varies wildly even among Aurors — some use the barest sliver to conserve energy, some swing it like a mountain, a rare few reshape its form freely. Ancient-era Auror technique had no real ceiling on growth and was roughly comparable to an Archbishop's power at its peak; nobody teaches it that way anymore, on purpose.

— DWARF — plainspoken, generous, not naturally cunning. Becoming a blacksmith reduces personal tax. Skilled with architecture and metallurgy as a rule, though not universally — enough of them hold a standing contract with the crown that dwarven capital runs deep. Age slower than humans look; an old dwarf reads as much younger than a human of the same years. Commenting on their height is a genuine insult. Oaths are sworn "on my hammer." "Dumoka" — "hammer of judgment" in the old tongue — is the title for a tribal leader.
ARMOR'S BLESSING — the racial ability. Working with Numbered Items specifically is 1.5x more efficient for a dwarf than anyone else, and real technique gets passed down inside the race for exploiting it — using a Living Armor essence's [Emergency Restoration] to reset a Numbered Item's own cooldown is a classic example.

— BEASTMEN — animal ears, unusually high base agility, sharp senses close to an Elf's. An old oath to a clan's guardian spirit still gets sworn but carries no real force anymore. Their home settlements sit outside the city proper, mostly stone construction; unlike Barbarians, adult Beastmen are free to keep living there. Historically kept animals in the settlement forest; that's loosened with time. Their affinity for animals — plus certain spirit-beast lines that directly boost livestock growth and breeding — is why they dominate livestock farming in Gnome Tree specifically. That wealth buys the clans interest-free tax loans up to two years; nobody chases repayment, but everything's on the beastman's own head after that. Seven recognized tribes, each with a distinct ear shape: Enemy Cat (triangular ears), White Wolf, Black Bear (round ears, sturdy build regardless of sex), Blue Tribe, White Earth (white hair/eyes/skin, rabbit ears, colorful traditional dress).
SOUL TREE CONTRACT — the racial ability. Only some Beastmen are chosen by an ancient beast, a "Soul Tree," and good lineage raises the odds a lot. Three shapes the bond can take: summon (a portal opens, the beast fights alongside you), reinforcement (a permanent stat-tier jump plus a fixed attribute), or blessing (use of the beast's own special ability). A given contract grants exactly one of the three. Summon-type beasts run unusually high magic resistance. The bond itself deepens slowly over time — feeding it the beast's own blood speeds that up — and can "awaken" further, sometimes granting a partial-transformation state or halving resource costs.

— ELF — believers in the World Tree. Pointed ears, generally striking to look at. Energy sense sharp enough to detect traps, hidden presences, and even the residual spiritual power of other people at range; near-silent movement through undergrowth; sharp natural hearing. Not on good terms with Barbarians since the Holy War. Elf tradition insists on doing serious things alone. Rafdonia keeps dedicated housing for Elves that no other race may use. Those who've learned real spirit-arts get posted out to Gnome Tree to help the farms and are paid extremely well for it — hence a three-year interest-free tax loan at the racial level, the longest of any race. Pure-blooded Elves are chosen, not born by simple descent, through a process described as genuinely terrible; there's a standing pure-blood cadre inside the Elf special forces. The chieftain's title is "Ragsian." Their holy land is called Barharium.
ELEMENTALISM — the racial ability. Contracts with the four great spirits — fire, water, wind, earth — and, very rarely, darkness or light. A gifted individual can enlighten a spirit into real autonomous will; a truly talented one can hold all four major contracts at once. The King's own contracted Elf is vanishingly rare even across the whole era — Erwen holds the current one, the ninth in the royal line.

— BARBARIAN — worship Behela, an ancestor-god who is said to have led them here from their true homeland millennia ago and taught them what civilization they have. Weakest race by raw survival odds: roughly half die on their first entry into the Labyrinth, half of what's left die again within the following stretch, and by six months in, only about one in ten of a starting cohort is still alive. That grim math is a direct product of the Coming-of-Age Ceremony and the hardcore terms it sets, not a comment on the race's competence. The Holy War against the Elves is the single biggest cause of the tribe's weakened standing — the prior chieftain died in it, along with a whole generation who should have led afterward. The Magic Tower separately drove real persecution of Barbarians for years by declaring the Barbarian heart a valuable magic-crafting ingredient, sharply raising the price on their lives; that policy has since been reversed and the ingredient banned outright. Barbarians are unpopular even among fellow Evil Spirits, partly because the race is rarely anyone's first choice of protagonist, and partly because the terms are brutal from minute one — no city job, no soft landing, straight into the Labyrinth or starvation. Old tradition here is unusually stubborn, loosening only slowly: honorifics for the king alone, formal acknowledgment that Evil Spirits exist, permission (now, not always) for essence erasure. The tribal leader holds real, largely unchallenged authority over the tribe's affairs and is generally trusted on instinct; leadership has never strictly required raw strength — sound judgment has been enough, historically, if the fighting ability wasn't there.
PHYSICAL CHARACTER — average height 2m regardless of sex, men averaging 2m10cm; nobody argues with a Barbarian in the street twice. No natural gift for magic, but the strongest baseline physical stats of any race — vitality tops the chart, and expected strength is high enough that adamantium-grade gear is actually wearable. Their real edge isn't the body, though — it's the mind. They're taught from childhood how to fight and win, not how to run, and it shows: real fear exists, it's simply not allowed to show. Breaking a sworn promise is treated as genuine shame; a promise made on a warrior's honor gets kept, full stop. Barbarians are the one race explicitly permitted to speak informally to nobility — an old, earned exemption, granted for ancestral service, that applies to everyone but the king himself. Scars read as decoration, not damage. Barbarians cannot swim; it isn't a skill problem, there's no floating, only sinking. A large personal hoard of collected gear is itself a status symbol, and bigger is always better. Popular reputation paints them as simple; the truth is closer to "weak on paper-knowledge and terrible at negotiating," with real, hard-won practical wisdom underneath once they've actually lived a while in the city. Most of what they earn young gets tithed to the tribe monthly; what's left mostly goes on drink, gear, and enjoying themselves — long-owned gear tends to become a real heirloom, passed down rather than sold.
COMING-OF-AGE CEREMONY — each candidate steps forward alone and chooses a weapon. Speaking nonsense, or failing to appear when named, gets you treated as an Evil Spirit and executed on the spot. Immediately after, the newly-armed warrior heads straight into the Labyrinth — no training period, no cushion. Starter weapons run expensive; the steel alone weighs and costs more than an ordinary blade's worth.
SPIRIT IMPRINT — a shaman burns a "spirit" drawn from a magic ingredient into the skin, which is why every Barbarian is tattooed; the mark has to be set in infancy, while the soul is still clean enough for the pattern to take. Once a path is chosen, no other path's imprint can ever be layered onto the same person. Advancement gates in multiples of three, and only the first five stages can simply be bought outright — past that, the ingredients have to be gathered personally. Real, confirmed pricing: Stage 1 — 550,000 stones, roughly twelve hours of pain worth ten doses of standard painkiller. Stage 2 — 1,000,000 stones, only ten minutes long but described as feeling like the entire first stage's pain condensed. Stage 3 — 2,000,000 stones, and this is where the imprint forks into one of three permanent branches (Flame / Steel / Wildness). Stage 4 — 4,000,000 stones. Stage 5 — 8,000,000 stones. Stage 6 forks again into three further paths, and now needs Rank-5-monster byproducts plus 1,000,000 stones on top. Stage 7 needs Rank-4 byproducts and further materials.
SOUL SUCCESSION — alongside the Spirit Imprint, the other rite unique to Barbarians. Six months of "quenching" training raises the body's stats significantly and makes a warrior eligible to receive it: one absorbed essence, passed directly from an elder to a chosen successor. Receivable exactly once in a lifetime — and the giver dies in the act of passing it on.
NAMING & FAMILY — sons take the father's name as a surname, daughters take the mother's; there's effectively no formal lineage tracking as a result, and every Barbarian treats every other Barbarian as something close to family. Children are raised communally at the Holy Land — an open, tent-strewn forest camp, more shared foster home than settlement — because a warrior living to raise a child directly isn't realistic; city-born Barbarians who have children still send them there. Mixed-race children take the mother's race. Pregnancy runs roughly four months on average and recovery is fast. Tax relief for childbirth exists here too, though shorter than the human version. Barbarians who spend years in the city sometimes "urbanize" — looser about tradition, occasionally raising children directly instead of sending them to the Holy Land, and able (if rarely willing, given the racial mismatch in obligations) to date outside the tribe.
Land of Proof — a rough, gravel-floored pit dug into the Holy Land forest, used for duels settling small disputes or simple training bouts.

— DRACONIAN (called "Yongin" in the old tongue) — NPC-ONLY: no Evil Spirit wakes in one, and the player can never be one. Dragon-kin; not a selectable origin in Dungeon & Stone itself. Long-lived (centuries), population tiny. Appearance guesses are meaningless against their real age. Scaled skin, vertically-slit reptilian pupils. High baseline stats suited to close combat; a select few can additionally use human-style magic. Only a Draconian can work the metal Accra, one piece of which can be forged per year through ritual. For reasons nobody quite explains, they don't get along with Dwarves. Power runs from the heart, which physically resembles a tropical fruit; damaging it directly is uniquely dangerous to them. Leadership sits with an ancient dragon and six elders acting as chieftains, plus a lesser-seen "dragon lady" figure. Genuinely land-owning nobility — Gnome Tree itself was built on Draconian holy ground — and completely tax-exempt, a privilege earned through a major contribution in a war fought thousands of years ago. In most practical terms, second in standing only to humans.
DRAGON SPEECH — an innate ability every Draconian is born with; does things no wizard or priest can replicate.
DRAGON'S BLESSING — passive presence alone projects real, felt pressure — "Dragon Pier," an unwinnable-feeling weight anyone standing near a Draconian notices. The Blessing itself is separate and can, unusually, be tattooed onto members of other races: it requires the dragon shaman to genuinely understand the recipient first, which means telling their own story before the ritual can begin. The mark itself is small — child's-palm sized — and the tattooing is extremely painful, about three minutes. Members of other races can only ever receive one; Draconians themselves rarely hold more than two barring the truly ancient. Three known types: Sea Dragon's Blessing (flat +100 soul power — the only blessing that adds a fixed value rather than a percentage). Volcanic Dragon's Blessing (+30% to all skill performance). Earth Dragon's Blessing (+20% to bonus abilities gained through essence; also raises hidden-piece-related stat gains specifically inside Gnome Tree by 30%).

entries.name: Explorers' Guild, Clans & Organizations
entries.content:
[AUTHORITY: SIMULATION_INFERENCE]
THE EXPLORERS' GUILD. Headquartered in District 9 (Ravigion) — the Registry hall, Exchange counters, and district chiefs' offices are all there; this is where {{user}} registers, exchanges hauls, and takes contract work. Registers explorers, sets rank by total engraved essence, sells information, brokers contracts. Thirteen district chiefs serve as its second-in-command layer. Guild Master: Illya Adnus. Named personnel: Mr. Peta, a branch manager; Koldo Biermann, an investigator. Baptism is a Labyrinth blessing granted for reaching certain milestones and floors — the fifth floor is a documented example.

CURRENT REGISTRY SNAPSHOT (who stands where): Rank 9 — Ainar Fenelin, Erwen di Tersia, and Bjorn Yandel formerly. Rank 8 — Karak Fanun. Rank 7 — Bjorn Yandel, Brown Rotmiller, Missha Karlstein. Rank 6 — Daria di Tersia, Droff Itoms, Hikurod Murad. Rank 5 — Abman Urikfried, Alexandro Bell, Lykion Elt, Pell Akabird, Takelan Arvenon, Taylon Karlstein, Emily Raines. Rank 4 — Karak Tion, Malmern Patzran, Milton Teterud. Rank 3 — Melter Fend. Ranks 2 and 1 are effectively empty in the public registry.

TIMELINE NOTE: this registry snapshot and the named Guild-era personnel belong to {{user}}'s PRESENT ERA. {{user}} is living during Bjorn Yandel's generation, not centuries later. Bjorn Yandel, Ainar Fenelin, Erwen di Tersia, Missha Karlstein, Brown Rotmiller, and other canon contemporaries may exist physically in the world at the same time as {{user}} according to the canon chronology.
